name: App architecture
routing_text: Structuring an application codebase: modular monoliths versus microservices, module and service boundaries, vertical slices, hexagonal ports and adapters, clean and onion architecture, domain driven design, coupling and cohesion, encapsulation, and keeping business logic out of the web framework.
blurb: How to cut an application into modules that survive contact with a team.

units.title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation
units.summary: Creators argue that monoliths should be reorganized into independent, interchangeable modules aligned with business capabilities rather than traditional layered structures. Concrete tactics include vertical slices or package-by-feature, explicit public APIs, information hiding, and using compiler or module frameworks to enforce boundaries. They also stress that dependency management goes beyond code to shared databases and conventions, and that domain subdomains (core, generic, supporting) help estimate change frequency. Simon Brown sees package-by-feature versus layer as debatable, while Kevlin Henney warns that hidden dependencies like JSON or database conventions can silently couple modules.

units.title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component
units.summary: A good monolith is a monolith that is easy to change, easy to modify, and easy to extend. Slices of functionality ensure exactly one request going in and one response coming out, with all logic in a single action class. Using microservices can make a system easier while the performance gets worse. Microservices are supposed to be independently deployable, unlike modules in a monolith, which are all deployed together in a single monolithic deployment.

units.title: AI and subtle craft define today's software engineering
units.summary: These creators portray modern software engineering as a mix of AI-driven tools and deliberate human judgment. They repeatedly mention design tokens, icon weights, animation feel, and AI agents—from LangChain to custom-built agents—as ingredients for quality, whether shipping dozens of PRs per day or preparing interview projects from hackathons. A point of tension: some advocate building agents from scratch before using frameworks, while others warn against discarding older engineering skills—but all agree the field is moving toward a higher-level, more intentional practice.

units.title: hexagonal architecture, layered architecture, ports and adapters, business logic, domain, place order
units.summary: Slicing your ports and adapters code into multiple source trees can stop infrastructure code from talking to each other at compile time. You could opt to remove the quantity check at the API level because it is also handled by the Pydantic model. The payments area should have a primary port. The SQLAlchemy inventory adapter gets the connection.

rubrics.criterion: Carve the codebase into modules around business functionality or axes of change, not into global technical layers.
rubrics.check: List the top-level packages/modules. If the first thing you see is controllers, services, repositories or other technical layers shared by all features, fail. Top-level modules should be named for business capabilities, and a feature change should live inside one such module rather than across every layer.
rubrics.why: In a technically-layered system a single change spans all layers and can affect unrelated functionality, so change becomes slow and risky to make.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

rubrics.criterion: Ensure every architectural construct you use to describe the system is first-class in the code.
rubrics.check: Take each module, component, layer or service named in the architecture diagrams or docs and locate it in source. If a name is only a conceptual grouping of interfaces and classes scattered across another layered structure, fail.
rubrics.why: A mismatch between the architecture description and the code means the diagrams stop working and the actual structure cannot be visualised, navigated or reasoned about.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

rubrics.criterion: Hide each module's design decisions behind an interface that reveals as little as possible and acts as a contract.
rubrics.check: Inspect each module's public API and its client code. Clients must depend on interface or contract types, not on implementation classes, and internal details such as data structures, external systems or algorithms must not appear in public signatures.
rubrics.why: If clients know the internals, every change to that hidden design decision ripples through all the clients; hiding the decision lets clients depend only on the contract.
rubrics.unit_title: Modular monoliths need vertical slicing and encapsulation

rubrics.criterion: Keep transport and persistence concerns out of domain logic.
rubrics.check: Scan the domain/business layer for imports or calls to the web framework, HTTP exceptions, API request/response types, and database connection or session types; fail on any occurrence.
rubrics.why: Mixing those concerns with domain logic couples the business to I/O, makes unit tests need mocks, and replaces domain language with transport details.

rubrics.criterion: Make each module independently changeable: a change inside a module must not force changes in other modules.
rubrics.check: Draw the module dependency graph; fail on cycles, references into another module's internals, or commits where one logical change edits files across module boundaries.
rubrics.why: When every change touches multiple modules, work becomes about not breaking the rest of the application instead of coding the feature.

rubrics.criterion: Do not claim 'modular' until explicit module boundaries exist.
rubrics.check: Look for enforced boundary rules: separate modules with public APIs, dependency constraints, or architecture tests; if none are present, fail the modularity claim.
rubrics.why: Renaming a monolith or microservices that are already a mess does not fix it; without boundaries the same tangled structure continues under a new label.

rubrics.criterion: Keep UI styles centralized in a design system or component library instead of duplicating styles per component.
rubrics.check: Scan the codebase for shared token references or a component library in dependencies; fail if the same style value (color, radius, spacing) is hardcoded across multiple components.
rubrics.why: Without tokens or reusable components, every change forces you to manually update each button and element, which scales badly and causes inconsistency.

rubrics.criterion: Include semantic color tokens (success, warning, danger, info) in the design system.
rubrics.check: Look at the token definitions or style dictionary; pass if semantic names like success, warning, danger, and info map to explicit values, fail if only raw palette hexes exist without semantic roles.
rubrics.why: Semantic tokens give UI states a consistent meaning instead of forcing developers to pick raw shade values for every alert, form, or status.

rubrics.criterion: Define fitness functions in CI that assert codebase quality metrics such as coupling and complexity.
rubrics.check: Check build and CI configuration for automated gates that fail when metrics like cyclomatic complexity or coupling exceed thresholds; pass if such checks exist.
rubrics.why: Fitness functions catch structural decay during the build so the team does not have to stop and schedule a refactoring sprint after shortcuts accumulate.

rubrics.criterion: Isolate domain and business logic from transport, HTTP and persistence framework concerns.
rubrics.check: In every unit that contains business rules, look for imports of web/HTTP frameworks, HTTP exceptions, database connections/session parameters, and response-shaped return types; any occurrence inside the domain layer fails.
rubrics.why: If business logic depends on a database or HTTP, tests need mock infrastructure and a domain concept cannot be expressed in its own language; changing persistence or transport framework forces changes to business code.

rubrics.criterion: Keep different modules or bounded contexts on separate data models and schemas.
rubrics.check: Find each relational table/collection or entity class shared by two modules, services or bounded contexts; if two units read/write the same table or one data model serves multiple business domains, fail.
rubrics.why: Shared schemas couple all consumers to one representation, so a change to one domain's data or rules requires hunting across every place that uses that model.
